" * Create a fraction given the double value and either the maximum error * allowed or the maximum number of denominator digits. *

* * NOTE: This constructor is called with EITHER - a valid epsilon value and * the maxDenominator set to Integer.MAX_VALUE (that way the maxDenominator * has no effect). OR - a valid maxDenominator value and the epsilon value * set to zero (that way epsilon only has effect if there is an exact match * before the maxDenominator value is reached). *

*

* * It has been done this way so that the same code can be (re)used for both * scenarios. However this could be confusing to users if it were part of * the public API and this constructor should therefore remain PRIVATE. *

* * See JIRA issue ticket MATH-181 for more details: * * https://issues.apache.org/jira/browse/MATH-181 * * @param value * the double value to convert to a fraction. * @param epsilon * maximum error allowed. The resulting fraction is within * epsilon of value, in absolute terms. * @param maxDenominator * maximum denominator value allowed. * @param maxIterations * maximum number of convergents. * @throws FractionConversionException * if the continued fraction failed to converge. "

"147 :     @Test
148 :     public void testDigitLimitConstructor() throws ConvergenceException {
152 : 
157 :         
158 :         // MATH-996
159 :         assertFraction(1, 2, new BigFraction(0.5000000001, 10));
160 :     }"

Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- Failing test: org.apache.commons.math3.fraction.BigFractionTest.testDigitLimitConstructor asserts that constructing new BigFraction(0.5000000001, 10) yields 1/2 (no exception).
- Constructor path: BigFraction(double, int) delegates to the private constructor BigFraction(double value, double epsilon, int maxDenominator, int maxIterations) with epsilon = 0, maxDenominator = 10, and maxIterations = 100.
- Core algorithm (continued fraction) in BigFraction(double, double, int, int) uses long intermediates p0, q0, p1, q1, p2, q2 and an overflow threshold set to Integer.MAX_VALUE.
- For a value very close to a simple fraction (0.5000000001 ≈ 1/2), the continued fraction contains a very large partial quotient. After the first two convergents (1, then 1/2), the next partial quotient becomes huge (on the order of 1/(value - 1/2) ≈ 2.5e9). This makes q2 leap beyond Integer.MAX_VALUE.
- At lines 303–307:
  if ((p2 > overflow) || (q2 > overflow)) {
      // in maxDenominator mode, ... return the last one.
      throw new FractionConversionException(value, p2, q2);
  }
  Despite the comment stating that in maxDenominator mode the code should “return the last one” when the next iteration would overflow, it instead throws a FractionConversionException.
- Because epsilon = 0 (maxDenominator mode), the intended behavior is to stop and return the previous convergent (p1/q1), which here is 1/2 and satisfies the maxDenominator constraint. Throwing an exception causes the test to fail.
- Why this only appears near simple fractions: Being extremely close to a simple rational makes a continued fraction term extremely large, pushing q2 above Integer.MAX_VALUE before the stopping condition (q2 < maxDenominator) can be applied, thus triggering the erroneous exception.
- Conclusion: The overflow branch in the private constructor’s continued-fraction loop incorrectly throws an exception in maxDenominator mode. It should instead stop the iteration and select the previous convergent (p1/q1), yielding 1/2 for 0.5000000001 with maxDenominator 10, as the test expects.

Based on the available information, provide the signatures of the most likely culprit methods for the bug. Your answer will be processed automatically, so make sure to only answer with the accurate signatures of all likely culprits (in `ClassName.MethodName(ArgType1, ArgType2, ...)` format), without commentary (one per line).
